title: Sea Ice Classification with Weakly Supervised Learning
text:
Preface
This Quarto Book provides background and resources for the NSF Funded Collaborations in Artificial Intelligence and Geosciences (CAIG) project Weakly Supervised Learning to Address Label-Data Irregularities in Sea-Ice Classification. This is a three year collaboration between University of Colorado Denver Computer Science and the National Snow and Ice Data Center (NSIDC).
The introduction provides an overview of the project. The Data section provides a description of the data used in the project. The Methods section describes our approaches to the problem.
NSF Award # 2531101
NSF Award # 2531102

title: 1  Introduction
text:
1.1 The Problem
Sea ice plays a critical role in the global climate system and maritime operations. Accurate and timely sea ice mapping and classification is essential for climate monitoring, navigation safety, and environmental decision-making. Manual sea ice mapping is slow and unscalable. Hence, the sea ice community is actively researching approaches to automate this process. Satellite imagery offers broad coverage of polar regions for data-driven automated sea ice classification; however, advanced deep learning methods for sea ice classification depend on labeled data, which are costly and time-consuming to generate. Despite significant advances in remote sensing and deep learning, the performance and reliability of sea ice classification models remain heavily constrained by the quality of the existing labeled data.
Almost all label data comes from ice charts produced by national ice information services such as the US National Ice Center (USNIC), Canadian Ice Service (CIS) and Danish Meteorlogical Institute (DMI). Ice Charts (along with other sea ice products) are produced

title: 2  Sea Ice
text:
2.1 Overview
Sea ice is any form of floating ice found at sea that has formed from the freezing of sea water. Sea ice is distinct from lake ice, which forms at the surface of freshwater lakes; river ice, which forms on the surface of rivers; and glacier ice that originates on land and may be found floating at sea as icebergs and ice shelves. Here we focus on sea ice.
Sea ice is split into two broad categories: fast ice, which forms at and remains along the coast; and drift ice, which includes all ice that is not fast ice. The term drift, refers to the ice’s ability to move freely. When concentrations are greater than 7/10, drift ice is normally referred to as pack ice.

title: 2  Sea Ice
text:
2.4 Stages of Development
The descriptions of the stages of development are taken from the WMO Nomenclature of Sea Ice and the Canadian ECCC MANICE. Many of the descriptions are based on the visual appearance of the ice, as well as the tickness. This reflects the history of ice observations being ship- or shore-based, and later from reconnaisance aircraft.

2.4.1 New Ice
Recently formed ice that icludes frazil ice, grease ice, slush, and shuga. The types of ice are formed from ice crystals that are only weakly frozen together.

Frazil Ice: fine spicules or plates of ice suspended in water
Grease Ice: a later stage of freezing where frazil ice crystals have coagulated to form a soupy layer of the surface. Grease ice does not reflect much light and gives the water surface a matte appearance.
Slush: Snow that is saturated and mixed with water on the sea ice surface or as a floating mass just after a heavy snowfall.
Shuga: spongy white ice clumps a few centimeters across. They are generally formed from grease ice or slush.



2.4.2 Nilas
A thin elastic “skin” (crust) of ice that flexes on waves and swell that grows as interlocking fingers. Nilas has a matte surface and may be up to 10 cm thick. Nilas is separated into dark nilas and light nilas.

Dark Nilas: nilas up to 5 cm in thickness and dark in color.
Light Nilas: nilas that is more than 5 cm thick and lighter in colour that dark nilas.
Ice Rind: a brittle, shiney crust of ice formed on a calm surface, either from direct freezing or from grease ice. It often occurs in water with low salinity. Ice rind is about 5 cm thick and easily broken into, usually, rectangular pieces by wind or swell.



2.4.3 Young Ice
Young ice is the transitional stage between nilas and first-year ice. It is between 10 and 30 cm thick. It is divided into grey ice and grey-white ice.

Grey Ice: Young ice between 10 and 15 cm thick. Grey ice is less elastic than nilas and breaks in swell. It usually rafts under pressure.
Grey-white ice: Young ice that is 15 to 30 cm thick. Under pressure, it is more likely to ridge than raft.



2.4.4 First Year Ice
First-year ice is sea ice that has no more than one winters growth. It develops from young ice and is more than 30 cm thick. First-year ice can be divided into _thin first-year ice (sometimes called white-ice), medium first year ice, and thick first year ice.

Thin First-year Ice/White Ice - First Stage: 30 to 50 cm thick
Thin First-year Ice/White Ice - Second Stage: 50 to 70 cm thick
Medium First-year Ice: 70 to 120 cm thick.
Thick First-year Ice: Greater than 120 cm thick.

title: 4  Data
text:
4.1 Overview
This section provides an overview of satellite instruments and data commonly used to estimate sea ice variables. Visible, near-infrared, and microwave sensors are used. Table Table 4.1 shows the wavebands for these sensors. However, because the polar regions are dark for part of the year and also the polar regions tend to be cloudy, microwave wavelengths are often preferred because they can operate during polar night and the atmosphere is largely transparent at these wavelengths (Figure 4.1).
Remote sensing instruments are either passive or active sensors. Passive sensors measure radiation from an external light source (e.g. the Sun or Earth) either reflected, scattered or emitted from a surface. Active sensors provide their own source of radiation and measure the reflected or backscattered signal.
Here we use focus on active sensors first, in particular Synthetic Aperture Radar.

4.2.2 Sentinel-1

4.2.2.1 Overview
Sentinel-1 is a C-Band radar. The Sentinel-1 mission was planned as a two-satellite constellation, with the two satellites sharing the same orbit plane. Sentinel-1A was launched on 3 April 2014. Sentinel-1B was launched 25 April 2016. Sentinel-1B was retired on 23 December 2021 because of a power supply issue. Sentinel-1C was launched 5 December 2024 and Sentinel-1D was launched November 2025.

Altitude: 693 km
Revisit Time: 6 to 12 days depending on regions

4.4.1 MODIS
The MODIS instrument on-board Terra and Aqua Satellites has MODIS Level 1B Calibrated Radiances for the 36 MODIS bands and reflectances for solar refelectance bands 1 through 19 and 26.
The MODIS sea ice algorithm uses the following bands from MOD02 MODIS Level 1B Calibrated and Geolocated Radiances. The sea ice algorithm uses the MODIS Land/Water mask, Solar zenith angle, geolocation, and Geoid height from MOD03, and the Unobstructed field of view and day/night glags from MOD35_L2 products.

Sea ice is assumed to be snow covered and is mapped based on a normalized difference of surface reflectances between bands 4 and 6, the Normalized Difference Snow Index.
\[
NDSI = \frac{band4 - band6}{band4 + band6}
\]
Pixels are identified as sea ice if the following criteria pass.

\(NDSI > 4\)
\(band2 > 0.11\)
\(band1 > 0.10\)

An Ice Surface Temperature (IST) product is also calculated. Surface radiances from bands 31 and 32 are first converted to brightness temperatures using a version of the Planck function.
\[
T_{\lambda} = \frac{c_2 \nu}{ln\left(1 + \left(\frac{e c_2 \nu^3}{E}\right)\right)}
\]
where \(T_{\lambda}\) is brightness temperature in \(\mathrm{K}\), \(\nu\) is central wavelength in \(\mathrm{cm^{-1}}\), E is radiance from the sensor in \(\mathrm{m\,W m^{-2}\,sr\,cm^{-4}}\), \(e\) is emmissivity, \(c_1\) is \(1.910659 \times 10^5\: \mathrm{m\, W m^{-2}\, sr\, cm^{-4}}\), and \(c_2\) is \(1.438833\: \mathrm{cm\, K}\).

4.4.3 Sentinel-2
Sentinel-2 is a multi-spectral imager.
Level 1C and Level 2A granules are 110 km by 110 km geometrically corrected ortho-images projected onto a Universal Transverse Mercator (UTM) CRS. Geometric corrections remove distortions from surface topography and imaging systems. Granules are designed to overlap.
Level 1C data are top-of-atmosphere reflectances. These data are based on Level 1B products that have been radiometrically corrected. Level 1C products include cloud masks and other QA grids.
Level 2A products are atmospherically corrected surface reflectance products derived from Level 1C products. In addition to surface reflectance, level 2A products include a Aerosol Optical Thickness (AOT) map, a Water Vapour (WV) map and a Scene Classification (SCL) map.

4.4.4 Sentinel-3
The main objective of the Sentinel-3 mission is to measure sea surface topography with the Altimetry Surface Topography Mission (STM), sea and land surface temperature with the Sea and Land Surface Temperature Radiometer (SLSTR), and ocean and land surface color with the Ocean and Land Colour Instrument (OLCI)..
Istomina et al. (2025) used OLCI and SLSTR channels to map melt ponds.

4.4.4.1 SLSTR
Channels: 2 channels in the visible (555 nm, 660 nm), a near-infrared channel (870 nm) and six thermal infrared channels (1370 to 12000 nm).
Swath width: 1470 km for nadir swath scanner and 740 km for oblique swath scanner.
Grid Size and Resolution: Nominal resolution of 500 m.
Temporal frequency: mean global revisit time is 1.9 days. For 3A and 3B the revisit time is 0.9 days at the equator.


4.4.4.2 OLCI
Channels: 12 channels in the visible wavelengths spanning 400 nm to 753.75 nm, and 9 channels in the near infrared spanning 761.25 nm to 1020 nm.
Swath Width: 1270 km
Grid Size and Resolution: the OLCI instrument has a 68.5\(^\circ\) field of view. The nominal spatial resolution is 300m
Temporal frequency: Orbital cycle is 27 days. Revisit time is 2-3 days.
